newsitem.title: UK: PolyGram sees swift restructuring benefits.
newsitem.headline: PolyGram sees swift restructuring benefits.

text.p: PolyGram NV is expecting the benefits of the 160 million guilder restructuring of its music operations to begin to feed through this year.
"They should be fairly short-term," PolyGram president and CEO Alain Levy said in an interview when asked when the benefits would be felt.
He said there should be some positive effects this year but added: "That is not essential. What is essential is to be adapted (to market conditions)".
PolyGram said last October it was cutting some 400 jobs positions worldwide as it responded to a sluggish music market.
PolyGram is restructuring the operations of its Motown unit, moving the label's headquarters from Los Angeles to New York as it seeks to recreate its heyday of the 1960s and early 1970s.
It is also reorganising its European music distribution and marketing operations in response to a flat market and restructuring its classical music division.
PolyGram said the global music industry grew by an estimated three percent last year, a marked slowdown after the rapid expansion of the past decade.
Levy said PolyGram believed the market could continue to grow at a rate of around five percent and said that creativity -- or rather a dearth of it -- had hit sales last year.
"In the U.S. you had a major sea change in taste," Levy said, noting that a number of major artists failed to sell the number of albums expected while younger acts took off.
He added that instability in the U.S. retail sector and difficult economic conditions in France and Germany had also contributed to the slump in sales growth.
Levy said he was "fairly optimistic" about the quality of PolyGram's music release schedule for 1997.
Albums from U2, Elton John and Van Morrison are in the pipeline while Levy said he was encouraged by the current success in Britain and France of the album by the band Texas.
PolyGram's Filmed Entertainment unit moved into profit in the second half of last year thanks to hit movies such as Sleepers, Mr Holland's Opus and Dead Man Walking.
"For a start-up operation it is doing extremely, extremely well," said Levy. "But we are now going into a second phase...with bigger budget movies. There will be ups as well as downs," he said.
